beats.lead: The first program to win a world title against humans never beat the champion.
beats.text: Chinook, a draughts program from the University of Alberta, finished second to Marion Tinsley at the 1990 US Nationals.
beats.note: All of its knowledge was programmed by its creators rather than learned.

beats.text: The governing bodies refused to let a computer play for the world title, so Tinsley resigned his title in protest and played the match anyway.
beats.note: He won in 1992 with four wins to Chinook's two, and 33 draws.

beats.context: the total number of games Tinsley lost from 1950 until his death in 1995. Two of them were to Chinook.

beats.text: In their 1994 rematch, all six games were drawn. Then Tinsley withdrew, ill with pancreatic cancer, and Chinook was declared champion.
In 2007 the same team proved that draughts, played perfectly by both sides, always ends in a draw.
beats.note: Published in Science as 'Checkers Is Solved'.

beats.line: The machine got the title. The man was never beaten.
